answers.answer: Bounce on fading volume is the earliest signal that beat random timing. It fires a median of 7 min after the high of day, 3.3% below it. Price fell 1 ATR before rising 1 ATR in 54.4% of 50,197 cases and did the opposite in 40.3%. That is +13.3 pts better than shorting at random moments at the same times of day (95% interval +12.4 pts to +14.1 pts). 1 of 21 signals beat random timing after correcting for testing 21 signals at once (5% false discovery rate).

For the signals that beat random timing (Bounce on fading volume), the edge was largest in the pre-market (+19.0 pts, interval +17.6 pts to +20.3 pts, 25,684 signals) and smallest before 10:00 (+5.1 pts, interval +2.3 pts to +7.7 pts). Many brokers restrict pre-market shorting; in regular hours it was best from 11:00 to 12:00 (+9.2 pts, interval +6.0 pts to +12.3 pts). Pooled across all signals, every time window did worse than random timing, because most breakdown signals fire right before a bounce. For 20 EMA turns from rising to falling → short a lower high below the 20 EMA; stop 3 atr above entry; no target (stop or time exit only); max hold end of day; entries 09:30-16:00, stopping new entries at 10:30 gave the most total profit: +0.09% per trade after costs, 39.4% winners, 42.4% of days positive, 1,319 trades. Before costs, the best cutoff for it was 10:30 (+1.16% per trade). In the first 60% of weeks the best cutoff was 10:30; in the last 40% it was 10:30 (the same answer). The best start/stop pair was 09:35 to 10:30 (+0.16% per trade over 1,294 trades). Trades entered in the 10:00 bucket averaged −0.36% (369 trades), the first 15-minute bucket with a non-positive average. A historical cutoff describes the average past trade; your own fills, size and discipline decide whether it applies to you.

Walk-forward test: each week was traded with the configuration that ranked best on the earlier weeks only. Out of sample that procedure averaged +0.49% per trade after costs over 549 trades (95% range −0.45% to +1.44%, so zero is still possible); 48% of the 96 test weeks were positive. It switched between 16 different configurations. Its most frequent pick (23 of 97 weeks) was 20 EMA turns from rising to falling → short a lower high below the 20 EMA; stop 3 atr above entry; no target (stop or time exit only); max hold end of day; entries 09:30-10:00. Before costs, the same procedure averaged +1.28% per trade (582 trades, 57% of test weeks positive). A typical short-listed trade paid 1.05% in costs: 0.71% spread and slippage, 0.04% commission and 0.30% locate. Ranked on the first 60% of weeks, the top configuration was First 1-min close below the 20 EMA → short a lower high below the 20 EMA; stop 3 atr above entry; no target (stop or time exit only); max hold end of day; entries 09:30-10:00. It earned +1.31% per trade there and +0.66% on the later weeks it had never seen (294 trades). 10 of the top 25 training-period configurations stayed positive out of sample. Its 2 neighbouring settings (one step tighter or looser stop, exit or hold) averaged +0.22% per trade against its own +1.02%, so it is an isolated peak, the usual sign of overfitting. Limited to trades a live screen could have caught (already under $1 with 1M+ shares by the entry minute, 54% of its trades), it averaged +1.09% over the whole period. Probability that the in-sample winner is below median out of sample (CSCV): 4% across 252 splits. 2,149,875 configuration-and-time-window combinations were tested, so the best in-sample number is optimistic by construction; rely on the out-of-sample figures.
